subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: What Is BIM? A Simple Guide to Building Information Modelling
subHeading: Understanding what BIM actually is, how it works and why it is much more than a 3D model.
abstract: BIM is a way of creating, managing and sharing information about a building or infrastructure project. Using a simple example, we explain how BIM connects people, models and information throughout a project's lifecycle.
body:
You may have heard people talking about **BIM**, but what does it actually mean?

BIM stands for **Building Information Modelling**.

At its simplest, BIM is a way of creating, managing and sharing information about a building or infrastructure project throughout its lifecycle.

And despite the name, **BIM is much more than a 3D model.**

## So, What Is BIM?

Imagine we're building a new apartment block.

An architect creates the architectural design. A structural engineer designs the foundations, columns, beams and slabs. Mechanical and electrical engineers design things like heating, ventilation, lighting and power.

A contractor then has to build everything on site.

Without a coordinated approach, each discipline can end up working with its own drawings, models and information.

BIM brings these different pieces of information together so that the project team can work from **coordinated and reliable information**.

The result is a digital representation of the asset that can contain both **geometry and information about the things being built**.

## It's More Than a 3D Model

A traditional 3D model might simply show us what a building looks like.

A BIM model can tell us much more.

For example, a wall might contain information about:

- Its dimensions and location
- What material it is made from
- Its fire rating
- Its construction type
- Its manufacturer
- Its relationship with other building elements

The model therefore becomes a place where information about the physical asset can be structured and managed.

Instead of simply seeing **a wall**, we can understand **what that wall actually is**.

## BIM Connects Different Disciplines

Let's go back to our apartment block.

The structural engineer has designed a beam.

The mechanical engineer has designed a ventilation duct.

If those two designs are developed independently, the duct could end up occupying the same space as the beam.

With coordinated BIM models, the teams can bring their information together and identify potential conflicts before construction reaches site.

The problem can then be resolved during design rather than discovered when someone is trying to physically build the system.

This is one of the major benefits of BIM:

> **Problems are often easier and cheaper to solve when they are found digitally before they become physical problems on site.**

## BIM Throughout the Project

BIM isn't only useful during design.

The information can develop as the project progresses.

During **design**, we might use BIM to understand the proposed building and coordinate different disciplines.

During **construction**, the information can support sequencing, quantities, fabrication and installation.

At **handover**, information about the completed asset can be provided to the owner or operator.

During **operation**, that information can help people understand, maintain and manage the building.

The model and information therefore have the potential to follow the asset throughout its lifecycle.

## What Makes BIM Different?

The important thing about BIM isn't simply that we have created a detailed digital model.

It's that the model is part of a wider **information management process**.

People need to know:

**What information do we need?**

**Who is responsible for producing it?**

**When is it needed?**

**Where is it stored?**

**Who needs to use it?**

These questions become increasingly important as projects become larger and more complicated.

## The Simple Definition

So, what is BIM?

You could think of it as:

> **A coordinated way of creating, managing and sharing information about an asset throughout its lifecycle.**

The 3D model is an important part of that process, but it is only one part.

BIM brings together **people, processes, information and technology** to help teams make better decisions about what they are designing, constructing and ultimately operating.

And that's the important distinction:

**BIM isn't about making a better-looking 3D model.**

**It's about managing information better.**

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: The Dimensions of BIM — What Do 3D, 4D, 5D and Beyond Actually Mean?
subHeading: Understanding how BIM moves from 3D geometry into time, cost, performance and the operation of an asset.
abstract: You may have heard of 3D, 4D, 5D and 6D BIM, but what do these dimensions actually mean? Using a residential apartment block as an example, we can see how additional layers of information build on the basic 3D model.
body:
You may often hear people talking about the dimensions of BIM — 3D, 4D, 5D and sometimes even 6D, 7D, 8D and beyond. But what exactly do these dimensions mean?

The terminology isn't completely standardised across the world. Different countries, companies and software providers can use the terms slightly differently. However, there are some conventions that apply broadly across the industry.

To understand the concept, let's take a simple example: **a residential apartment block**.

We can start with a three-dimensional model of the building and progressively add more information to it. Each additional "dimension" represents another way of using information about the asset.

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: What Is LOD in BIM? Understanding Level of Detail
subHeading: A simple guide to understanding how a BIM element develops from an early concept into a detailed representation of the finished asset.
abstract: LOD describes how much graphical detail has been developed in a BIM model. Using a drainage pipe as an example, we follow the journey from a simple conceptual representation through to detailed construction and the installed asset.
body:
You may have come across the term **LOD** when talking about BIM. It stands for **Level of Detail**, and it is essentially a way of describing how much graphical detail has been developed in a model element.

Put simply:

> **LOD tells us how much detail we have modelled.**

But what does that actually mean?

Let's take a simple example — **a drainage pipe running through our residential apartment block**.

As the project develops, our understanding of the drainage system improves. The model therefore becomes progressively more developed.

**This is the basic idea behind LOD.**

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: What Is LOIN in BIM? Understanding Level of Information Need
subHeading: A simple guide to understanding what information a BIM model actually needs to contain, and why that information changes throughout a project's lifecycle.
abstract: LOIN defines the information actually needed from a BIM model for a particular purpose. Using a fire door as an example, we look at how the required geometry, data and documentation change from design through construction and into operation.
body:
You may have come across the term **LOIN** when talking about BIM. It stands for **Level of Information Need**.

Put simply:

> **LOIN tells us what information we actually need about something, and when we need it.**

The idea is simple: don't produce more information than you need, but don't leave out information that someone actually needs to do their job.

## What does LOIN actually mean?

LOIN is about defining the information required from a BIM model for a particular purpose at a particular point in a project.

That information can broadly be thought of in three areas:

- **Geometry** — what the object looks like, its size and location
- **Information** — data attached to the object
- **Documentation** — drawings, manuals, certificates and other supporting documents

Let's take a simple example — **a fire door in our residential apartment block**.

## One Door, Different Information Needs

At the early design stage, the architect might only need to know:

- Where the door is
- Its approximate size
- That it is a fire-rated door

That's enough to develop the design.

Later, the contractor needs more information.

They might need:

- Exact dimensions
- Fire rating
- Door type
- Manufacturer or product specification
- Installation requirements

After the building is completed, the facilities team may need something different again:

- Asset ID
- Manufacturer
- Model
- Serial number
- Warranty information
- Maintenance documentation

The **door hasn't changed**.

What has changed is **the information that people need from it**.

That's the basic idea behind LOIN.

## Why Do We Need LOIN?

BIM projects can contain an enormous amount of information.

The problem is that **more information isn't automatically better**.

If a model contains hundreds of properties that nobody needs, someone still has to create, check, maintain and update all of that information.

LOIN gives us a way to ask:

> **What information is actually needed for this purpose, at this point in the project?**

Instead of simply asking someone to "add more information", we can define exactly what is required.

This helps avoid both **too little information and unnecessary information**.

## LOIN vs LOD

This is where LOIN is often confused with LOD.

**LOD is mainly concerned with the graphical development of an element.**

For example:

> How accurately and completely have we modelled this fire door?

LOIN asks a broader question:

> **What information do we actually need about this fire door?**

That could include the geometry, but also the data and documents associated with it.

So you could think of it like this:

**LOD**

→ *How developed is the modelled object?*

**LOIN**

→ *What information about that object do we actually need?*

The two ideas work together, but they aren't the same thing.

## The Key Idea

LOIN is ultimately about **giving the right person the right information at the right time**.

For our fire door, that might mean:

**Design:**
*We need to know where it is and what type it is.*

**Construction:**
*We need to know exactly what we're installing.*

**Operation:**
*We need to know what asset we've got and how to maintain it.*

The goal isn't to fill the BIM model with as much information as possible.

**It's to provide the information that actually has a purpose.**

subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: Who Are the Parties in BIM? Understanding Appointing Party, Lead Appointed Party and Appointed Party
subHeading: A simple guide to understanding who asks for information, who coordinates it and who produces it on a BIM project.
abstract: BIM projects involve different organisations with different responsibilities for producing and managing information. Using a simple apartment building example, we explain the roles of the appointing party, lead appointed party and appointed party.
body:
You may have come across some slightly confusing terminology when reading about BIM:

**Appointing Party.**
**Lead Appointed Party.**
**Appointed Party.**

They sound complicated, but the basic idea is actually quite simple.

They're essentially different roles within the **chain of responsibility for producing and managing project information**.

Let's use a simple construction project to see how they fit together.

## The Basic Relationship

Imagine a client wants to build a new apartment block.

The client appoints a main contractor to design and construct the building.

The main contractor then appoints a number of specialist companies — perhaps a steelwork contractor, MEP contractor and façade contractor.

You can think of the relationship like this:

**CLIENT**

↓

**MAIN CONTRACTOR**

↓

**SUBCONTRACTORS / SPECIALISTS**

Each party has a different role in the information process.

## The Appointing Party

The **appointing party** is essentially the organisation receiving the information.

In our example, this is the **client**.

The client might say:

> "I need information about the building that allows me to understand what is being designed, constructed and eventually handed over to me."

The client therefore establishes what information is required and makes appointments with the organisations responsible for delivering it.

Think:

> **"I need this information."**

The appointing party is often the client, owner or employer, although it doesn't always have to be. The important thing is the role they are performing in that particular appointment.

## The Lead Appointed Party

The **lead appointed party** is the organisation directly appointed by the appointing party and responsible for coordinating information within its delivery team.

In our example, this could be the **main contractor**.

The client appoints the main contractor to deliver the project.

The main contractor then has to coordinate the information produced by the different teams working under its appointment.

For example:

- Structural contractor
- Steelwork contractor
- MEP contractor
- Façade contractor
- Specialist suppliers

The main contractor therefore isn't necessarily producing all the information itself.

It is responsible for **coordinating the information coming from the delivery team and providing the required information to the client**.

Think:

> **"I'm responsible for coordinating this information and getting it to the client."**

## The Appointed Party

The **appointed party** is the organisation providing information as part of the delivery team.

For example, our main contractor might appoint a specialist steelwork contractor.

The steelwork contractor could be responsible for producing information about:

- Steel members
- Connections
- Fabrication
- Installation
- Quantities
- Relevant specifications

They provide that information to the party that appointed them.

Think:

> **"I'm responsible for producing this information."**

## Putting It Together

Let's imagine our apartment building again.

The relationships could look something like this:

### Client

**Appointing Party**

> "I need the information required to deliver and operate my building."

↓

### Main Contractor

**Lead Appointed Party**

> "I'll coordinate the information from my delivery team and provide it to the client."

↓

### Steelwork Contractor

**Appointed Party**

> "I'll produce the information about the steelwork I'm responsible for."

↓

### Steel Fabricator

**Appointed Party**

> "I'll provide the information required for the fabrication of the steel."

The exact structure can become much more complicated on a large project, with multiple delivery teams and layers of appointments.

But the basic principle remains the same.

## One Important Detail

Here's where the terminology can initially become confusing.

**The same organisation can have different roles in different appointments.**

For example, imagine the main contractor has been appointed by the client.

In that relationship:

**Client → Main Contractor**

The client is the **appointing party** and the main contractor is the **lead appointed party**.

But the main contractor then appoints a steelwork contractor:

**Main Contractor → Steelwork Contractor**

Now the main contractor is the **appointing party for that appointment**, while the steelwork contractor is the **appointed party**.

So the terminology describes **the role being performed within a particular appointment**, rather than giving every company a permanent BIM title.

This is one of the most important things to understand.

## Why Does BIM Use These Terms?

The terminology helps make responsibility clearer.

Instead of simply saying:

> "The contractor needs to provide the model."

we can ask:

**Who is appointing them?**

**What information are they responsible for?**

**Who coordinates that information?**

**Who ultimately needs to receive it?**

This becomes particularly important on large projects where hundreds of organisations may contribute information to the overall project.

## The Simple Version

If you remember nothing else, remember this:

**Appointing Party**

→ **"I need the information."**

**Lead Appointed Party**

→ **"I'll coordinate the information and deliver it to you."**

**Appointed Party**

→ **"I'll produce the information I'm responsible for."**

The terminology might sound complicated, but the underlying idea is simply about **who asks for information, who coordinates it, and who produces it.**
